package_info.why_malicious: The report discusses multiple malware campaigns and attack techniques, including malicious Android apps (such as those masquerading as COVID-19 trackers and the Tekya malware family), DNS hijacking leading to phishing, exploitation of Adobe Type Manager Library vulnerabilities via malicious font files, and the use of LNK shortcut files to deliver payloads. No single package from a package manager is analyzed in detail; instead, the report highlights various methods attackers use to deliver and execute malicious code.

execution_context.file_location: Android app APK masquerading as 'Coronavirus Finder'

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: After infection, a web page called 'Coronavirus finder' shows the number of people infected around the victim’s location, and urges them to pay a small sum to see their exact location, thus stealing credit card data.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the app displays a fraudulent infection map, prompts the user to enter credit card details, transmits the entered payment data over the network to an attacker-controlled server, resulting in theft of sensitive financial information.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The app impersonates a legitimate COVID-19 tracker to socially engineer users into providing credit card information, which is then exfiltrated to an attacker.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate health or tracking app should not request payment information under false pretenses or transmit sensitive data to unverified servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate apps may request payment for premium features, but do so transparently and securely, not as part of a scam or with intent to steal.
key_indicators: Fake infection map used as a lure
Unsolicited request for credit card information
Transmission of payment data to untrusted remote server
Masquerading as a COVID-19 tracking application

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after DNS hijack and browser navigation)
execution_context.file_location: Malicious web page delivered via DNS-hijacked router

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The DNS rerouting results in opening a web page presumably from the World Health Organization (WHO), luring the victim to download malicious content.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, following unauthorized DNS changes, the user's browser is redirected to a phishing page impersonating the WHO, which prompts the user to download a malicious app, leading to further device compromise.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The web page is delivered as a result of unauthorized DNS manipulation and impersonates a trusted organization to distribute malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DNS settings should not redirect users to phishing or malware sites, and reputable organizations do not distribute apps via unsolicited redirects.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate organizations may provide downloads on their official sites, but not via DNS hijacking or deceptive redirects.
key_indicators: Phishing page visually imitating WHO branding
Prompt to download unverified or malicious app
Delivery of malware via compromised network infrastructure

execution_context.file_location: Android app from Google Play Store (Tekya malware family)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The malware obfuscates native code to avoid detection by Google Play Protect and utilizes the ‘MotionEvent’ mechanism in Android to imitate the user’s actions and generate clicks.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the app executes obfuscated native code that simulates user clicks using the MotionEvent API, generating fraudulent ad interactions and exfiltrating ad revenue to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The app conceals its true purpose through code obfuscation and simulates user input to commit ad fraud, which is not a legitimate use of accessibility or input APIs.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate apps do not obfuscate code to evade detection or simulate user input for fraudulent ad revenue generation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Accessibility services may simulate input for users with disabilities, but not for the purpose of ad fraud or evasion.
key_indicators: Evasion of Google Play Protect and other security tools
Unusual ad traffic patterns originating from the app

execution_context.trigger: file preview (import-time in Windows Explorer preview pane)
execution_context.file_location: Malicious document with embedded PostScript Type 1 font (Adobe Type Manager Library vulnerability)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The vulnerabilities relate to the Adobe Type Manager (ATM) library, which manages PostScript Type 1 fonts. The flaws can be exploited when the victim views the files in 'preview mode' using Windows File Explorer, without even opening the malicious document.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, a specially crafted PostScript Type 1 font embedded in a document triggers a remote code execution vulnerability in the Adobe Type Manager Library, allowing arbitrary code execution when the file is previewed in Windows Explorer.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The font file is intentionally crafted to exploit a vulnerability and execute code without any user interaction beyond previewing the file.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Previewing a document or font file should not result in code execution or compromise of the system.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason for a font file to execute code during preview; font files should only be used for rendering text.
key_indicators: Maliciously crafted PostScript Type 1 font embedded in document
Triggers code execution via Windows Explorer preview pane
Exploits Adobe Type Manager Library vulnerability

execution_context.file_location: Windows LNK shortcut file (created by mLNK builder tool)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The tool does so by converting payloads to LNK shortcuts.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when the LNK file is opened, it executes an embedded malicious payload, bypassing traditional security solutions and enabling arbitrary code execution on the victim's system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: LNK files are abused to conceal and execute malware payloads, leveraging the trust in shortcut files to evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate shortcut files should not contain or execute hidden malware payloads upon opening.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: LNK files are used for legitimate shortcuts to applications or documents, but not for covert payload delivery or code execution.
key_indicators: LNK file with embedded executable payload
Execution of hidden code upon shortcut activation
Bypasses traditional security and detection mechanisms

attack_chain.action: User is lured to install a malicious app, open a malicious file (APK, font file, LNK shortcut), or visit a phishing web page delivered via DNS hijack.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code or payload is delivered to and executed on the victim's device.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes, resulting in credential theft, data exfiltration, ad fraud, or remote code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Theft of sensitive data, financial loss, device compromise, or further malware propagation.

attack_chain.action: Malware attempts to evade detection through code obfuscation, anti-analysis techniques, or by leveraging trusted file types (e.g., fonts, LNK files).
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence on the victim's device and continued malicious activity without detection.

behavioral_signatures: Android apps requesting payment or credit card information under false pretenses
Unauthorized changes to router or device DNS settings resulting in redirection to phishing or malware sites
Obfuscated native code in mobile apps that simulates user input or generates automated ad clicks
Font files or LNK shortcuts that trigger code execution upon preview or open, especially via Windows Explorer preview pane
file_indicators: APK files masquerading as COVID-19 or health-related apps
LNK shortcut files with embedded or hidden executable payloads
Malicious PostScript Type 1 font files embedded in documents
Unexpected or unauthorized changes to router or device DNS configuration
network_indicators: Exfiltration of credit card or credential data to untrusted or attacker-controlled servers
Connections to domains or IPs impersonating the World Health Organization or other trusted entities
Unusual or excessive ad traffic patterns originating from mobile devices or specific apps
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for installation of suspicious APKs, especially those requesting sensitive information or masquerading as health apps. Detect unauthorized changes to DNS settings on routers and endpoints. Analyze execution of LNK and font files for signs of code execution during preview or open events. Use behavioral analysis to identify apps simulating user input or generating fraudulent ad clicks. Inspect network traffic for exfiltration of sensitive data to untrusted domains and for connections to domains impersonating trusted organizations. Employ endpoint protection capable of detecting obfuscated code, payloads hidden in non-executable file types, and abuse of trusted file formats.
